title: Acute infectious diarrhoea and dysentery in adults (India)
specialty: Internal Medicine / Infectious Diseases / Emergency Medicine / Primary Care

evidenceAudit.scope: Acute watery diarrhoea and dysentery in adults and adolescents in India: dehydration assessment, oral and IV rehydration, when to give antibiotics, amoebic dysentery and avoidance of fluoroquinolones, using NCDC-ICMR NTG 2025 section 4.2 and WHO rehydration plans. Childhood diarrhoea and cholera have separate topics.
findings: Antibiotics only with danger signs (azithromycin 500 mg once daily for 3 days first line; cefixime 400 mg twice daily or ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily for 5 days), stool microscopy in dysentery with metronidazole 400 mg three times daily for Entamoeba histolytica, and avoidance of fluoroquinolones because of high resistance in India checked against NCDC-ICMR NTG 2025 section 4.2.

Dehydration signs, Plan A ORS 300 mL per loose stool (over 20 kg), Plan B 75 mL/kg over 4 hours, Plan C Ringer lactate 100 mL/kg (30 mL/kg in 30 minutes then 70 mL/kg over 2.5 hours from 12 months of age), reassessment and fluid-overload signs checked against the WHO plans (MSF Appendix 14).
unverifiedSections: The WHO plans in the opened source are written for children; Plan B volumes above 30 kg and Plan C timing for adults are extrapolated from the 12 months and older column.
NTG 2025 does not define 'danger signs' in the opened extract; usual signs (high fever, blood in stool, severe dehydration, sepsis, immunosuppression) are listed as practice.
Metronidazole duration for amoebic dysentery is not in the opened extract.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Acute infectious diarrhoea in adults is usually viral or from toxin-producing bacteria and settles in a few days with fluids alone. The main danger is dehydration and electrolyte loss; dysentery (blood and mucus) suggests invasive bacteria such as Shigella or Campylobacter, or Entamoeba histolytica. Most adults do not need antibiotics; NTG 2025 reserves them for patients with danger signs and advises against fluoroquinolones because resistance is high in India. Oral rehydration solution (ORS) treats mild and moderate dehydration; severe dehydration needs rapid IV Ringer lactate.
keyMechanisms: Enterotoxins (for example from E. coli, Vibrio) drive chloride and water secretion: watery diarrhoea.
Invasive organisms damage the colonic mucosa: dysentery with blood and mucus.
Fluid loss causes hypovolaemia, acidosis and hypokalaemia.
Glucose-coupled sodium absorption remains intact, so ORS works.

symptoms: Loose watery stools, vomiting, abdominal cramps
redFlags: Severe dehydration: lethargic, unable to drink, skin pinch over 2 seconds, no urine for hours (WHO)
Blood in stool with high fever or sepsis
Rice-water stools with rapid dehydration: suspect cholera (see Cholera topic)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Profuse rice-water stools, rapid severe dehydration; see Cholera topic.
Persistent fever more than diarrhoea; blood culture.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Normal mental state, eyes and skin pinch; drinks normally.
Restless, sunken eyes, skin pinch goes back slowly, thirsty, reduced urine (2 or more signs).
Lethargic or unconscious, unable to drink, skin pinch over 2 seconds, no urine for hours (2 or more signs).

ruleIn.normalValue: Alert, normal skin pinch, drinking normally
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Two or more signs of some or severe dehydration
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Chooses WHO Plan A, B or C.

clinicalManagement.title: Rehydrate
actions: Plan A: ORS after each loose stool, about 300 mL (over 20 kg) (WHO).
Plan B: ORS 75 mL/kg over 4 hours, then reassess (WHO).
Plan C: Ringer lactate 100 mL/kg: 30 mL/kg in 30 minutes then 70 mL/kg over 2.5 hours; repeat the first part if pulse still weak (WHO).

clinicalManagement.title: Monitor
actions: Record signs and vitals every 15–30 minutes until stable for 1 hour (WHO).
Watch for fluid overload: rising respiratory and heart rate, crackles, oedema (WHO).
Start ORS 5 mL/kg/hour once able to drink (WHO).

clinicalManagement.title: Antibiotics only if indicated
actions: Avoid fluoroquinolones: high resistance in India (NTG 2025).
Dysentery: stool microscopy; treat E. histolytica with metronidazole (NTG 2025).

branches.label: Diarrhoea with danger signs
branches.entryCriteria: Severe illness, high fever, bloody diarrhoea with systemic features, or admission.

regimens.dose: Plan A: about 300 mL after each loose stool; Plan B: 75 mL/kg over 4 hours
regimens.frequency: After each stool (Plan A); continuous small sips (Plan B)
regimens.duration: Until diarrhoea stops; reassess Plan B at 4 hours
adjustments: Paediatric: Children by weight: under 5 kg 50 mL, 5–10 kg 100 mL, 10–20 kg 200 mL per stool (WHO).
Penicillin allergy: Not an antibiotic; penicillin allergy does not change this medicine.
CKD: Caution in kidney failure (sodium and potassium load).
CLD: No adjustment.
contraindications: Severe dehydration or unable to drink: use IV

medicationPlan.note: Antibiotics only for danger signs, as in NCDC-ICMR NTG 2025 section 4.2; avoid fluoroquinolones. Rehydration volumes from WHO plans (MSF Appendix 14). India-only topic; the Saudi topic is unchanged. Not clinically reviewed.

learningObjectives: Grade dehydration and choose Plan A, B or C.
keyPoints: Fluids first: ORS or Ringer lactate.
Plan C: 100 mL/kg Ringer lactate in about 3 hours.
Antibiotics only for danger signs; azithromycin 500 mg daily for 3 days (NTG).

patientEducation: Drink ORS after every loose stool.
Return for blood in stool, inability to drink, drowsiness or little urine.
Wash hands with soap after toilet and before food.
